extracted.intended_audience: employers, legal practitioners, policymakers, labor researchers, and public commenters on the FTC non-compete rule
extracted.subtask_description: Extraction of the FTC's final-rule standards, definitions, and evidentiary findings concerning non-compete and functionally-equivalent contractual provisions, including how harms to labor markets and commerce are assessed and how different clause types are treated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'functional non-competes'
rubrics_metrics.description: The final rule uses the term “functional non-competes” to convey that certain terms are considered non-competes under the final rule where they function to prevent workers from seeking or accepting other work or starting a business after their employment ends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The NPRM used “de facto non-competes,” but the final rule prefers “functional non-competes.” The Commission gives examples (discussed elsewhere) such as liquidated-damages clauses with prohibitive magnitudes, overly broad NDAs, forfeiture-for-competition clauses, and similar contractual terms that operate to bar post-employment work or entrepreneurship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unfair methods of competition (scope)
rubrics_metrics.description: Unfair methods of competition include practices that are “collusive, coercive, predatory, restrictive, or deceitful” as well as “exclusionary.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Ethyl and the FTC Policy Statement. This is the substantive lens the Commission uses to assess practices under Section 5—whether a practice is an unfair method of competition given its character and effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 5 showing: burden on a not insignificant volume/portion of commerce
rubrics_metrics.description: A practice may be unlawful under Section 5 where the Commission finds the practice unfairly burdened competition for a not insignificant volume of commerce; the Commission finds that the use of non-competes substantially affects commerce and burdens a not insubstantial portion of commerce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Atlantic Refining, Texaco, and other cases: it is enough that the Commission found the practice unfairly burdened competition for a not insignificant volume of commerce; proof of foreclosure of a relevant market is not necessary in the exclusive-dealing context.

rubrics_metrics.name: No acceptance of firm-level justifications to excuse otherwise illegal practices under Section 5
rubrics_metrics.description: Justifications based on advantages to individual firms (economic benefits to the company) cannot excuse an otherwise illegal business practice under Section 5.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Atlantic Refining, Texaco, and L.G. Balfour Co. v. FTC. The Commission will similarly not accept justifications for claims pursued through Section 5 where courts have not accepted such justifications under the antitrust laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liquidated damages provisions can be de facto non-competes
rubrics_metrics.description: Liquidated damages provisions in an agreement may operate as de facto (functional) non-compete clauses when they specify prohibitive magnitudes of damages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Wegmann v. London and Brown v. TGS Mgmt. Co., LLC as examples where courts treated liquidated-damages clauses as de facto non-competes because of their prohibitive magnitudes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overbroad NDAs may operate as de facto non-competes
rubrics_metrics.description: An NDA that defines “confidential information” so broadly as to prevent a person in perpetuity from doing any work in a field can operate as a de facto non-compete and therefore be unenforceable under some state law regimes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Brown v. TGS Mgmt. Co., LLC and TLS Mgmt. & Mktg. Servs. v. Rodriguez-Toledo. The Commission treats such overly broad confidentiality provisions as functional non-competes in its analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forfeiture-for-competition clauses treated as functional non-competes
rubrics_metrics.description: Forfeiture-for-competition clauses (contract terms that forfeit pay/benefits upon post-employment competitive activity) are considered by the Commission as potentially functioning like non-competes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters provided business justifications for such clauses; the Commission addresses those justifications separately (Part IV.D.2). Examples and the Commission’s evaluation of such justifications are discussed elsewhere in the rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Garden leave may restrict post-employment mobility
rubrics_metrics.description: The practice of “garden leave” (asking an employee not to come into work during the notice period) is a recognized practice that can functionally restrict a worker during separation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Noted that the term and practice has a British origin and is recognized by the UK Government (Gov.UK). The Commission references garden leave as a practice with potential restrictive effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical finding: non-competes harm labor-market outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: The evidence establishes that non-competes affect labor mobility, workers’ earnings, new business formation, and innovation, including empirical evidence identifying cross-border effects with respect to earnings and innovation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission summarizes studies in Parts IV.B and IV.C (and cites Treasury and academic studies—e.g., Johnson, Lavetti, & Lipsitz; Starr et al.; others). These findings underpin the Commission’s conclusion that non-competes substantially affect commerce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Behavioral/chilling effects even where non-competes are unenforceable
rubrics_metrics.description: Available evidence shows workers are chilled from engaging in competitive activity even where a non-compete is likely unenforceable—because they may be unaware of the law or unable to afford litigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This phenomenon implies enforceability-based studies may understate real-world effects; the Commission notes that its notice requirement (§910.2(b))—requiring employers to notify workers that their non-compete is no longer in effect—could amplify observed effects by reducing worker ignorance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of empirical literature: correlation vs. causation
rubrics_metrics.description: Many empirical analyses should be interpreted as descriptive or correlational rather than causal; cross-sectional variation in enforceability may be correlated with other unobserved differences across states.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission repeatedly cautions about causal interpretation (citing Starr, Prescott, & Bishara; Johnson & Lipsitz; authors’ own disclaimers). This is guidance for weighing and interpreting the studies cited in the rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate treatment for senior executives versus other workers
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission distinguishes non-competes with workers other than senior executives (referred to simply as “non-competes” in Part IV.B) from non-competes or covenants that apply to senior executives (addressed in Part IV.C), with definitions in §910.1 and specific provisions in §910.2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The findings about harms apply with respect to senior executives and other workers, whether considered together or respectively; the rule defines and treats senior-executive coverage separately (see §910.1 and §910.2 references).

rubrics_metrics.name: Antitrust law connections: non-compete agreements as subjects of Section 1 scrutiny
rubrics_metrics.description: Employee non-compete agreements can be proper subjects for scrutiny under Section 1 of the Sherman Act; agreements among competitors to allocate territories or payments to stay out of the market may violate the antitrust laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites cases like Palmer v. BRG of Ga., Inc.; United States v. Topco Assocs.; FTC v. Actavis; Newburger, Loeb & Co., Inc. The Commission notes that non-competes can impede efficient allocation of labor and tie up industry expertise in ways that raise antitrust concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enforceability-study bias: measured effects may understate true harms
rubrics_metrics.description: Studies that assess changes in enforceability of non-competes likely underestimate the effects of non-competes because workers may refrain from seeking or accepting work (or starting a business) even where a non-compete is likely unenforceable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission uses this point to explain why the final rule (including notice requirements) could have larger effects than those observed in enforceability-focused studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-competes can impede reporting of employer illegality and increase illegal conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments summarized by the Commission state that non-competes increase illegal conduct by employers and make it harder for workers to report illegal conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission references Part IV.B.3.a.iii for a summary of these commenters and their claims; this is treated as one of the harms associated with non-competes in the rulemaking record.
